decisions.quote: The PHQ-15 subscales and the total score were positively and significantly correlated with COVID-19 anxiety, as well as with GAD-7 total score. These correlations are in line with results from the first wave of the UK study [20].
decisions.reason: Row 259 targets Shevlin et al. (2020) [20] (10.1111/bjhp.12430) on COVID-19-related anxiety predicting somatic symptoms. In Section 3.1 (lines 37-39) and the Discussion (line 43), the authors report that PHQ-15 total and subscale scores were positively and significantly correlated with COVID-19 anxiety in line with [20], that higher COVID-19 anxiety predicted more severe somatic symptoms in Models 1 and 2 (with a more linear increase across quintiles and a similar wider effect in the 5th quintile), and that pre-existing health problems and high GAD-7 scores worsened somatic symptoms, 'confirming UK's findings.' Under the codebook, a difference in functional shape or effect magnitude does not make a supported finding mixed. The shipped 'mixed' coding and quote pertained to the other re-tested UK study [19] (10.1192/bjo.2020.109) on anxiety, depression, and traumatic stress rather than [20].

corrected_value.title: Anxiety, depression, traumatic stress and COVID-19-related anxiety in the UK general population during the COVID-19 pandemic.
corrected_value.authors: Shevlin, M.; McBride, O.; Murphy, J.; Miller, J.G.; Hartman, T.K.; Levita, L.; Mason, L.; Martinez, A.P.; McKay, R.; Stocks, T.V.A.; et al.

decisions.quote: Summarizing, these results are in line with those of the UK study about anxiety, depression, and traumatic stress [19]. The UK and Italian data identify factors associated with worst psychological health: being a woman, younger age, having children, preexisting health issues of self or someone close, and the moderate to high perceived risk of contracting COVID-19 within one month. Unlike Italy, in the UK lower household incomes and having (had) the COVID-19 were associated with worst psychological health outcomes.
decisions.location: Discussion, line 49 (see also Aims, line 14; Analytic Methods, line 34; Discussion, line 44; References, line 288)
decisions.reason: Omitted target. The paper explicitly re-tests two distinct UK C19PRC empirical papers [19,20]. In Section 3.2 (line 34, 41) and the Discussion (line 44: 'In a second part of the analysis, we replicated the approach by Shevlin et al. [19]'), the authors replicate the three binary logistic regression models from Shevlin et al. (2020) [19] (10.1192/bjo.2020.109) in the Italian sample and report mixed results (line 49: several risk factors matched the UK study, whereas lower household income and having had COVID-19 were associated with worse outcomes in the UK unlike Italy). Because [19] is an independent published paper whose findings are directly re-tested, it must be coded as a separate replication target.
